existing_incident_edges.relationship: Technologies to exploit coal as Europe’s difference: China Transformed (1997) followed “arguments of E. A. Wrigley”, as Wong recalled in 2016
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Wong, “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ 26:3, 2016, p. 76, read): “The cluster of differences stressed in that work concerned European science and technologies, and in particular, following arguments of E. A. Wrigley, the importance of technologies to exploit coal as a source of energy to power new kinds of machines”; his note cites Continuity, Chance and Change (1988). Qualification: this is Wong’s retrospective account. China Transformed is read only in chapter openings, and the passage that cites Wrigley there was not read. Wrigley’s own organic-economy argument is on e_a_wrigley → capitalismdebates (edge_1084).

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Reciprocal comparison of China’s and Europe’s advanced regions: Pomeranz followed “a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed”, with “greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures” (2000)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Pomeranz’s own words, The Great Divergence (2000, pp. 7–8, later-edition preview, read): a regional approach “anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong” (p. 7); “Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed … viewing both sides of the comparison as ‘deviations’ when seen through the expectations of the other, rather than leaving one as always the norm” (p. 8); “my concrete application of this reciprocal comparative method has some significant differences from Wong’s”, with “greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures and reciprocal influences” (p. 8 and n. 13). Readers: Parthasarathi (2011, p. 5): “Kenneth Pomeranz builds upon this work”; Huang (2002, p. 520) traces Pomeranz’s use of the industrious revolution to “R. Bin Wong’s brief discussion earlier (1997, 30–31)”. Wong (Comparativ 2016, read): Pomeranz rejected “numerous putative differences … including my China Transformed” (p. 73); China Transformed “followed the same method” (p. 76); both books “shared … the basic problem of non-falsifiability” (p. 77). The same debt is recorded as the strand global/reciprocal_comparison_resources (carried by edge_898); this arrow makes it a relationship between the two entries.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: From the limits of European experience to political scale: with Rosenthal, Wong argued that European fragmentation and warfare concentrated manufacturing in cities, where higher wage costs favoured labour-saving techniques (2011, as Wong summarised in 2016 and Ma reported in 2012); in 2016 he recast divergence from “why Britain” to a more general transformation
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words, “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ 26:3, 2016, pp. 77–78, read): “Rosenthal and I ended up focusing on an important political difference between China and Europe – political fragmentation in Europe and the presence of an unitary state for the Chinese empire”; war gave “craft producers an incentive to locate in cities”; “We turned the issue of divergence from a question of why was Britain the first industrializer to why was industrialization more likely to occur in Western Europe than in China” (p. 77); “By making the question of the great divergence a more general one we recognize that even a profoundly transformative process like modern economic growth could take place in several ways and begin at several locations” (p. 78). Before and Beyond Divergence (2011) is unread; Ma’s review (EH.Net 2012, read in full in revision 1.145) reports the same dichotomy of “a unified and centralized imperial China versus a politically fragmented Europe” and the mechanism: warfare brought “a greater degree of concentration of trade and manufacturing in urban locations”, and, “With higher urban wages”, innovation in Europe “would be more biased towards saving labor than in China”. Ma finds this “stimulating and striking hypothesis” “supported by fairly meager evidence in the chapter”, and the evidence on public goods “even shakier”. He also reports the authors’ challenge to “the accepted thesis of China being a high interest rate and capital scarce country”, and judges the book “a good contribution in the Great Divergence debate” for addressing “some of the key issues beyond what has been done recently by Pomeranz, Allen and others”, though “far less so when it comes to providing credible support for its own thesis”. The wage mechanism is Ma’s report; Wong’s 2016 summary gives the move of craft production to cities. Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014, p. 16.2) say Rosenthal and Wong “adopted” Allen’s induced-innovation argument “wholesale”. China Transformed (1997), as Mokyr quotes it, held that the “supply-driven Industrial Revolution that followed the demand-led Industrious Revolution in Europe did not happen in China” (p. 31); Mokyr objected that “Bin Wong does not cite any book by Needham” (2002 draft, pp. 3–4). The co-authored argument is Rosenthal’s as well as Wong’s.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Brenner’s agrarian social relations, like Pomeranz’s coal and colonies, are traits particular to Britain, so that their necessity “cannot be falsified” (2016)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Wong, “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ 2016, pp. 74–75, read): “when my colleague and Marxist historian Robert Brenner famously argues that it is the absence of the agrarian social relations found in Britain that prevented the emergence of capitalism elsewhere, the importance of the system through which he sees the modern world economy emerging cannot be falsified because the enclosures and the social relations that attended them were particular to Britain. Like Pomeranz’s coal and colonies, Brenner cites traits that are British and not present elsewhere” (p. 74); “Neither the scientific revolution nor agrarian social relations lend themselves very easily to counterfactual exercises because they are themselves so large and encompassing” (p. 75). He allows that such traits “could in fact be factors helping to explain the industrial revolution” (p. 75). A methodological critique in one passage, citing the Aston and Philpin collection; it does not dispute Brenner’s evidence. Brenner’s other respondents are on capitalismdebates → robert_brenner (edge_1078), which does not name Wong.
existing_incident_edges.map_label: Wong questions the falsifiability of Brenner’s explanation, 2016

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Mokyr argues that Wong leaves the intellectual foundations of technological divergence insufficiently explained.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own October 2002 draft, 2–4, describes Wong’s comparison as unresolved, then criticizes the absence of Needham from China Transformed and demands fuller explanation of useful knowledge and technological change. At 4 he also agrees with Wong that Smithian growth alone cannot explain the transformation. Wong’s book is not newly read or independently audited here; this is Mokyr’s attributed criticism, distinct from the Pomeranz coal-and-land criticism already on edge_1110. The preliminary conference draft is not equated with a published book or proof of conference delivery.

named_group_routes.relationship: Reciprocal comparison of Eurasian cores, joined to connections in a polycentric world (2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own statement of method, The Great Divergence (2000), introduction (pp. 3–27 read; later-edition pagination). Comparisons between scattered core regions should be 'truly reciprocal' (p. 8), 'viewing both sides of the comparison as “deviations” when seen through the expectations of the other, rather than leaving one as always the norm' (p. 8). With Tilly's 'encompassing comparison', 'comparison and the analysis of connections become indistinguishable' (p. 10). 'Thus the book combines comparative analysis, some purely local contingency, and an integrative or global approach', and before 1800 'we have, instead, a polycentric world with no dominant center' (p. 4). The introduction ends 'with connections and interactions explaining what comparison alone cannot' (p. 25). He places the book as 'joining the burgeoning field of “world history,”' while warning that it 'treats the world’s regions very unevenly' and that 'adding a few Chinese and Japanese foils to a European story does not make it “world history”' (p. 25). A contribution, not a founding: the approach was 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong' (p. 7), and 'Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed' (p. 8); the encompassing comparison is Tilly's (p. 10, n. 14). Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for this edge. Revision 1.144: later reception of the method. Pomeranz was a co-founding editor of the Journal of Global History, which began publication in 2006 (AHA biography, as the second research pass reads it). Its editors wrote in 2021 that the Great Divergence debate "was a major inspiration for the foundation of the Journal in 2006" and that "comparisons and connections" had been "elaborated perhaps most fruitfully in the context of large-scale reciprocal comparisons" (Frankema, Sood and Tworek, JGH 16:1, pp. 1–2, read in full by the second pass); they do not name Pomeranz.

named_group_routes.relationship: Reciprocal comparison as the California School's method: Wong (1997), Pomeranz (2000) and Parthasarathi's 'parallels in Eurasia' (2011), read by Vries as 'a new kind of comparative reciprocal history that suits global historians' (2013)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Pomeranz (2000, pp. 7–8, read): a regional approach 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong'; 'Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong's recent China Transformed … viewing both sides of the comparison as "deviations" when seen through the expectations of the other'. Parthasarathi (2011, publisher excerpt): earlier explanations 'all identify something that made Europe different … This book takes a different approach … it rejects claims for European difference' (p. 1); 'Kenneth Pomeranz builds upon this work' (p. 5). Vries (2013, pp. 14–15, read): 'The Californians, moreover, experiment with a new kind of comparative reciprocal history that suits global historians who not only want to juxtapose but also connect.' The method strands stay on global/comparison and global/reciprocal_comparison_resources.

named_group_routes.relationship: The “industrious revolution” applied to Chinese household labour (2000), and de Vries’s 1976 book cited as “a good general critique of the overseas extraction thesis”
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Pomeranz’s own words, The Great Divergence (2000; later-edition preview, read): labour deployment in Chinese families “seems to closely resemble the reorientation of labor, leisure, and consumption toward the market that Jan DeVries has called Europe’s ‘industrious revolution’” (p. 17; n. 28 cites DeVries 1994b); the contents list a section “Family Labor in China and Europe: ‘Involution’ and the ‘Industrious Revolution’”; “A good general critique of the overseas extraction thesis is DeVries 1976” (p. 3 n. 2). Huang (JAS 2002, pp. 520–521, read in revision 1.144) reads the borrowing critically: “it is surprising that Pomeranz would have tried to equate the Yangzi delta with de Vries’ industrious revolution”, “along the same lines as R. Bin Wong’s brief discussion earlier (1997, 30–31)”; “he tries to take the revolution out of de Vries’ industrious revolution.” The use is Pomeranz’s; de Vries’s own later judgement of The Great Divergence (Historically Speaking, 2011) is unread and not drawn. The Huang–Pomeranz dispute over involution is on edges 1043–1044.
